text:
The Harbour Lights Festival

Every August the small river town of Wexcombe fills with musicians, and this year was no different. The town sits on the River Severn, about two hours west of London by train, and for one long weekend its population of four thousand grows to nearly thirty thousand. The festival began in 1987, when a retired schoolteacher named Agnes Pollard borrowed a flatbed lorry from the Wexcombe Brewery and parked it beside the old ferry landing. She invited three local bands to play. One of them, a folk group called The Tidewater Boys, still closes the festival every Sunday night.

This year the opening act was Maya Okafor, a singer from Lagos who now lives in Bristol. She played for an hour under a light rain, and the crowd sang every word of her song "Salt and Iron" back to her. Afterwards she told a reporter from the BBC that Wexcombe reminded her of the fishing towns she knew as a child. "It's the same smell of diesel and seaweed," she said. "I feel at home here."

The main stage belongs to the Harbour Lights Trust, a charity that took over the festival from Agnes Pollard in 2004. Its director, Tom Ashworth, says the trust spends most of its money on safety and on the free children's tent. "People think a festival is about the headliners," Ashworth said on Saturday morning. "It's really about toilets, water and first aid." The trust works closely with the St. John Ambulance volunteers, who treated about two hundred people this year, mostly for sunburn on Sunday afternoon.

On Saturday the crowd was biggest for Glass Pilots, a four-piece band from Manchester. Their second album, Northern Weather, reached number six in the U.K. charts last spring. Their singer, Dan Whitlock, wore a borrowed fisherman's jumper and a hat from the Wexcombe Rowing Club. Midway through the set he stopped to thank "Mrs. Pollard", as everyone in town still calls her, and the crowd cheered for almost a minute. Pollard is now eighty-one. She watched from a folding chair beside the sound desk, holding a paper cup of tea.

Not every act was British. The Canadian fiddler Louise Tremblay flew in from Montreal by way of Dublin, and a jazz trio from New Orleans played two sets in the Anchor Tent. The trio's leader, Marcus Bell Jr., has recorded with musicians on three continents. He said he first heard about Wexcombe from a documentary on Channel 4. "I saw a town that loved music more than money," he said, "and I wanted to see it for myself."

The festival also has a quieter side. In the Mill Room, a converted flour mill beside the weir, writers read from new books. On Saturday afternoon the novelist Helen Marsh read the first chapter of The Lantern Keeper, her novel about a lighthouse family on the Isle of Man. She was followed by the poet Idris Vaughan, who read in Welsh and then in English. The room held about sixty people, and many more stood outside the open windows to listen.

Food at the festival comes mostly from local farms. The Severn Valley Growers cooperative runs a long market along the quay, and the bakery on Chapel Street sells out of pasties by noon every day. This year the market added a stall run by students from Hartley College, who sold soup to raise money for a new minibus. They raised just over two thousand pounds.

Music lessons are a newer part of the weekend. Every morning at nine, teachers from the Royal Northern College of Music run free workshops for beginners in the Methodist Hall on Bridge Road. This year about three hundred children learned to play a simple tune on the tin whistle, and on Sunday they marched through the town behind Billy Rowe and his accordion. Parents lined the pavement to film them, and the shops along the high street put flags in their windows.

The weekend was not without trouble. On Saturday night a storm blew in from the west, and the organisers closed the main stage for forty minutes while a crew tied down the lighting rig. A spokesperson for the Environment Agency said the river rose by almost a metre overnight, but it stayed below the flood wall. Some campers on the low field moved their tents to the cricket ground, which the Wexcombe Cricket Club opened for free.

By Sunday morning the sky had cleared. Families walked along the towpath to the Old Toll Bridge, where a brass band from Cornwall played hymns and film tunes. A boy of about seven asked the bandleader to play the theme from Star Wars, and the band obliged, a little out of tune. Nearby, volunteers from the Royal National Lifeboat Institution let children climb into an inflatable rescue boat.

The closing night belonged, as always, to The Tidewater Boys. Only one of the original members, the accordion player Billy Rowe, still plays with the group. The others are younger musicians from Gloucester and Hereford. They played for two hours and finished with "The Ferryman's Daughter", the song Agnes Pollard asked them to play at the very first festival. When the last note faded, the lights on the harbour wall came on one by one, as they have every year since 1987.

Tom Ashworth says next year's festival will be the largest yet. The trust has already booked Maya Okafor to return, and it hopes to add a second stage on the far bank of the Severn. It also plans a small exhibition in the Wexcombe Museum on the history of the festival, with photographs lent by families in the town. The trust asks anyone with old programmes, posters or recordings to contact its office on Quay Street.

For Agnes Pollard, the growth of the festival is both a pleasure and a worry. "I never meant it to be big," she said. "I only wanted the town to hear some good music on a summer night." Then she finished her tea, folded her chair and walked slowly home along the river.
